TBH pricepoint is everything. Humble bundle establishes that quite clearly. If all of those new release games were $20-30, they'd be making significantly more profit. Granted, there would still be people too poor to pay, and people who aren't going to buy it on principle of the company not committing to their customers, but those people weren't going to buy anyways. Those are not lost sales. The people who can't afford it, or who don't see the value return in shelling out every time a new AAA comes out because they -all- cost $60-80 are the sales that they actually lost. Those are the real hits to their bottom line.

Or if the DRM on the paid version breaks the game. But yeah, I buy plenty of old games that I could easily get ROMs for. Hell, I'll buy an old PS2 game and then run a ROM of it for the enhanced graphics while still paying for the game.
True. There's lots of instances where people who legally buy a game, get shafted by the drm meant to affect pirates.

Let's be honest, the DRM isn't meant to stop piracy or they'd have given up since every DRM setup gets cracked extremely quickly. The DRM is there to allow them to do things like activation limits or having to connect to a server at launch so that they can screw people into needing a new copy of the game or to upgrade to the latest sequel.
And the funny thing about DRM is that all it does is limit those options. Players will seek out software that doesn't have always-online requirements and DRM software.

Ease of access is the driving factor here. A perfect example would be the new Rare Replay that just came out. Download thirty games to your console in ten minutes and have all controls set up to play sounds good. Finding a Mame emulator online somewhere, then finding the ROMs and finally finding a controller and getting it set up properly sounds like a lot of work. I can do it but I'm not a Noob. 95% of the population would rather take the easy route. At least here in the U.S. where we are kind of lazy and procrastinate a lot.

This is the biggest answer.

If you want people to not pirate, you have to make it more convenient and easier to actually buy the game. Thanks to things like Virtual Console on the Wii, remakes of classic games on other consoles, and an ever-growing market of used games, it's easier to buy old games now than it was when they were new. People are also starting to get tired of the modern era of recycled game components and a lot of people are reaching back for the classics they know and love. Overall, it's great to see that people are keeping the past alive, and this is a great illustrating point in the motivations behind piracy. We're not all greedy fucks, some of us are just very careful with our money and don't like to buy things that will waste our time or we're not sure will be worth the money. Retro games have already vetted those tests time and time again, so they're always a safe bet.

I will admit as a teenager I pirated the hell out of things. I just didn't have the money to get games/software. Now that I'm in my 30's, I try to buy when possible. I've been playing a lot of older games lately. Especially old RPGs and strategy games, and it's incredible how well a lot of them hold up. It's also sad that they aren't all available except through the secondary market. Like the oldest Wizardry games, or the Gold Box series of RPGs. You also end up with the inferior DOS ports of games that originally premiered on the Apple II. For example, I'm convinced the RNG in the DOS port of Wizardry is broken. And apparently the DOS port of Akalabeth (maybe better known as Ultima 0?) is severely gimped the game by removing its unique, randomly generated dungeons. Sadly, those are the versions people are most likely to play.

On the plus side, these older RPGs offer something modern RPGs don't. The ability to beat them inside of 20 hours.
I'm a little surprised on this not being here already, but allow me to answer http://m.quickmeme.com/img/ca/ca3ccee4598511757877635d40222f7c92a5cfd4ec2d7cb8151896ff9e610339.jpg

IMO, one of the best things Nintendo did with the Wii was the Virtual Console. It helped make up for the lack of original downloadable titles, but it went beyond that.

From late 2006 through 2008 alone, the Wii got over 220 retro games, for $10 each at most. Casual fans of a series or company could more easily look back into their old archives, often enjoying it for the first time while supporting the publisher. People could play the NES Mega Man games alongside 9 and 10, Super Mario Bros 3 and Super Mario World alongside New Super Mario Bros, Ocarina of Time alongside Twilight Princess, Sonic on the Genesis along with Sonic Colors, and so on. And later on the 3DS, we got the same thing again with the Game Boy and Game Boy Color. If it weren't for the 3DS Virtual Console, I wouldn't have been able to play Maega Man V, Shantae, Mole Mania, Kirby's Dream Land 2, Pokemon Trading Card Game, or Mario Golf.

Sure, ROMs are free. But most people are willing to spend a few dollars.

This highlights one of the biggest misconceptions about why people pirate: We don't want media for free, we want media period. If it's fairly priced, convenient, and worth buying, we'll buy it; if it doesn't meet these criteria, we won't. It is as simple as that. This is how Steam, GOG, Spotfy, Pandora, Netflix, etc, etc have taken off in recent years. It's also why I haven't pirated anything that is available on the streaming or gaming services that I subscribe to in a very long time.

Well, think about it... If I can go to a place that sells retro games, or look on Amazon or eBay or something, the average SNES game might cost 10 or 15 bucks. It's a lot easier to think 'yeah, I'ma get this' impulsively when a game is less than $20, instead of fuckin' $60.
